title: Reverse burden of proof under NDPS - the constitutional challenge
p1: Can a person be asked to prove their innocence before the prosecution proves their guilt? This question lies at the heart of one of the most debated issues under the NDPS Act.
p2: Many believe that in every criminal case, the burden always remains only on the prosecution. But under certain NDPS provisions, once specific facts are established, the accused may have to explain how they came into possession of a prohibited substance. This shift is called the reverse burden of proof.
p3: The challenge is about balancing two important values: controlling serious drug offences and protecting the fundamental right to a fair trial. Courts have examined whether these provisions create an unfair disadvantage for accused persons or whether they are justified due to the difficulty of proving hidden drug networks. The key takeaway is that reverse burden does not remove the prosecution's duty completely; the initial facts still matter.
conclusion: Do you think reverse burden provisions under NDPS are necessary for effective law enforcement, or do they risk weakening the presumption of innocence?
